articles.title: Ordinary names, specific names, and two nouns together

article_json.also_called: Common nouns, proper nouns and compound nouns
article_json.one_line: This lets you tell an ordinary naming word from the name of one particular thing, and write a two-word name correctly.
article_json.short_answer: Ordinary names stay lower case: *a city*. The name of one particular thing takes a capital: *Norland*. In a two-noun name the first noun stays singular.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: Which naming words take a capital letter, and can I put two of them together?

body.text: Two sorts of naming word, written two different ways
A noun names something. Most nouns name a kind of thing, so they fit any member of that kind: *a river*, *a college*, *a delay*. These stay lower case wherever they sit in a sentence.

A smaller group names one particular thing and nothing else: *Norland*, *Tuesday*, *March*. These take a capital letter every time, because the capital is what marks them out as the name of one thing.

body.caption: A capital letter marks the name of one particular thing.
rows: a river runs through the town
the Ashfield runs through the town
the new college opened in May
footnotes: Languages, nationalities and the names of subjects taught as courses also take a capital: *Arabic*, *Norwegian*, *Environmental Science*.

body.lead_in: Only the naming word changes here. Watch the capital letter follow it.

items.text: A new footbridge opened last spring.
items.gloss: Some footbridge somewhere opened. You are not saying which.

items.text: The Marlow footbridge opened last spring.
items.gloss: One particular footbridge opened, and you have named it.

items.text: Two of the volunteers study engineering.
items.gloss: They are engineering students.

items.text: Two of the volunteers study at Brackenfield.
items.gloss: They study at one particular place, and you have named it.

body.so_what: The capital letter is not decoration. It tells the reader you mean one particular thing, not a kind of thing.

body.text: Two nouns together, where the first one describes the second

English packs meaning by putting one noun in front of another. The second noun is the thing you are talking about. The first one narrows it down, so *traffic congestion* is congestion, and *energy policy* is policy.
When one noun describes another, put it in front, and leave it singular. Any plural ending goes on the second noun.

body.lead_in: Only the number of things changes here. Watch which noun takes the *-s*.

items.text: The council published its energy policy in June.
items.gloss: One policy about energy is now public.

items.text: Three councils published their energy policies in June.
items.gloss: Three separate policies about energy are now public.

items.text: Traffic congestion is worst on the ring road.
items.gloss: The traffic backs up there more than anywhere else.

items.text: We need a bicycle rack outside every station entrance.
items.gloss: There should be somewhere to leave bicycles at each station.

body.so_what: The first noun never takes *-s*, however many things there are. The count lives on the second noun.

body.text: What goes wrong with names and two-noun groups

body.wrong: The report compares three energies sources across the county.
body.right: The report compares three energy sources across the county.
body.why_it_happens: There are three of them, so the plural ending feels as though it should go on both words. In English the first noun is doing the work of a describing word, and describing words never take *-s*.
body.smallest_fix: Take the *-s* off the first noun. Leave it on the second.

body.wrong: The Norland is the fastest growing town in the county.
body.right: Norland is the fastest growing town in the county.
body.why_it_happens: *The* points at one particular thing, and a place name already does that on its own. Adding *the* is saying the same thing twice, so English leaves it out.
body.smallest_fix: Delete *the* in front of the name of a town, a city or a person.

body.label: Three place names that keep *the*, and they are a closed set

items.text: Country names that are plural or that contain an ordinary noun keep *the*.
items.example: The Netherlands sent two observers to the conference.

items.text: Rivers, seas, oceans, deserts and mountain ranges keep *the*.
items.example: The delta has widened by half a kilometre since 2015.

items.text: Buildings and organisations named with *of* keep *the*.
items.example: The University of Sandmouth runs the survey every autumn.

body.heard: A noun is the name of a person, a place or a thing.
also_known_as: nouns are naming words for things you can touch
body.truth: That misses most of the nouns in an essay. *Progress*, *a decision*, *the meeting* and *unemployment* are all nouns, and none of them is a person, a place or a thing you can touch.
body.what_to_do: Use a test instead of a meaning. If you can put *the* or *a* in front of the word, or add *-s* to it, it is a noun.

body.headline: Capital for one particular thing. First noun singular.

article_json.no_practice_reason: No practice point covers ordinary and specific names or two-noun compounds. They are written conventions the reference alone carries.

articles.title: Things you can count, and things you cannot

article_json.also_called: Countable and uncountable nouns, and the nouns that are both
article_json.one_line: This decides whether a noun can take *-s*, whether it can take *a*, and which word for amount goes in front of it.
article_json.short_answer: Ask whether you can say *two* of it. *Two reports*, yes, so it takes *a* and *-s*. *Two informations*, no, so write *information* alone or *a piece of information*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I know whether a word can take *-s* and *a*?

body.text: One question decides three things about a noun

Put *two* in front of the noun and say it out loud. *Two reports* works. *Two equipments* does not. That single test tells you whether the noun can take *-s*, whether it can take *a*, and which word for amount goes with it.

body.gloss: things you can count one by one / stuff you measure

show_first.text: The panel received four reports and one letter.
The site needs new equipment before the winter.
Two of the applications arrived after the deadline.

body.name_line: A noun you can count is **countable**. A noun you measure instead is **uncountable**.
body.anchor_line: *Reports* and *applications* come in ones you can point at. *Equipment* comes in an amount, so English never counts it directly.

body.caption: The answer to *can I say two of it?* settles the rest.
footnotes: *Some*, *any*, *a lot of*, *plenty of* and *no* go with both, which is why they are the safe choice when you are unsure.

body.lead_in: Only the noun changes here. Watch what has to change around it.

items.text: The tutor gave me three suggestions about the draft.
items.gloss: She made three separate points about my writing.

items.text: The tutor gave me some advice about the draft.
items.gloss: She told me what to do about my writing.

items.text: Many households now heat their water with a heat pump.
items.gloss: Heat pumps are common in homes now.

items.text: There isn't much evidence that the scheme reduced traffic.
items.gloss: Almost nothing shows that the scheme worked.

body.so_what: Nothing moved except the noun, and the noun dragged the word for amount and the verb ending with it.

body.text: The ten nouns that look countable and are not

Some nouns name something that arrives in separate pieces, so they feel countable. English still treats them as an amount. The list below is short and it is worth learning as a list, because each one is highly visible when it goes wrong.

body.caption: None of these ever takes *-s* or *a*. All of them take *is*.
footnotes: *Furniture*, *luggage*, *homework*, *traffic*, *transport* and *weather* behave the same way.
*Researches* and *trainings* do occur in some technical and institutional writing. Treat all ten as uncountable and nobody will mark you down.

body.text: To count an uncountable noun, count the container instead: *a piece of*, *an item of*, *a body of*, *two pieces of*.

body.lead_in: Same noun each time. Only the counting phrase in front of it changes.

items.text: The tutor left one piece of feedback on each section.
items.gloss: She wrote one comment per section.

items.text: The depot ordered six items of safety equipment.
items.gloss: Six separate pieces of kit are on the way.

items.text: A growing body of research links air quality to absence rates.
items.gloss: More and more studies show the same link.

items.text: Can you send me a bit of information about the deadline?
items.gloss: You want to know when the deadline is.

body.so_what: The noun never changes. The phrase in front of it does the counting.

body.text: Nouns that are both, and the meaning moves when they switch
A group of nouns sits on both sides. The two versions are not the same word used loosely. They mean different things, and the *a* or the *-s* is what tells the reader which one you mean.

body.caption: Adding *a* or *-s* changes what the word refers to.
rows: what you have learnt by doing
*a paper* = an article, or a newspaper
*works* = a factory, or an artist's output
footnotes: *Chicken*, *iron* and *coffee* work the same way: the material against one object or one serving.

body.lead_in: The same noun twice. Only *a* or *-s* changes, and the meaning moves with it.

items.text: She has ten years of experience in transport planning.
items.gloss: She has been doing this work for ten years.

items.text: Cycling to the depot in February was an experience.
items.gloss: It was one memorable occasion, and not a comfortable one.

items.text: The engineer published a paper on flood defences.
items.gloss: She wrote one article and it came out.

items.text: The wrapping is made from recycled paper.
items.gloss: The material it is made of has been used before.

body.so_what: One small word decides whether you mean the stuff or one particular item of it.

body.text: What goes wrong when the test is skipped

body.wrong: The team collected many evidences from three different sites.
body.right: The team collected a great deal of evidence from three different sites.
body.why_it_happens: The evidence arrived in separate pieces, so it feels countable, and *many* asks for a plural. English stores *evidence* as an amount, so the counting has to move to a phrase in front of it.
body.smallest_fix: Drop the *-s* and change *many* to *a great deal of* or *a lot of*.

body.wrong: My supervisor gave me an advice about the second draft.
body.right: My supervisor gave me some advice about the second draft.
body.why_it_happens: It was one thing she said, so *an* feels right. *An* means one countable item, and *advice* is not counted in ones, so English uses *some* or *a piece of* instead.
body.smallest_fix: Replace *an* with *some*, or write *a piece of advice*.

body.wrong: The amount of students applying has risen sharply since 2019.
body.right: The number of students applying has risen sharply since 2019.
body.why_it_happens: *Amount* and *number* both mean how much there is, so they feel like the same word. *Amount* goes with things you measure and *number* goes with things you count.
body.smallest_fix: Count the noun. If you can say *two* of it, use *the number of*.

body.mechanism: Russian marks how many by changing the ending of the noun and the words around it, and there is no separate word for *a*.
body.wrong: Council published informations about the closure.
body.right: The council published information about the closure.
body.fix: Choose the word in front of the noun first, then leave the noun alone.

body.heard: Uncountable nouns are things you cannot see or touch.
body.truth: Meaning does not decide it. *Furniture* and *luggage* are things you can carry, and both are uncountable. *An idea* and *a decision* are things you cannot touch, and both are countable.
body.what_to_do: Ignore what the thing is like. Say *two* in front of the noun. If that sounds wrong, treat the noun as uncountable, whatever it names.

body.headline: Say *two* in front of it. That answer decides everything else.

table.caption: One row per outcome of the test.

body.note: Answers are shown. Nothing here is recorded and nothing is marked.

items.prompt: Fix this: *We need more furnitures for the reading room.*
items.answer: *We need more furniture for the reading room.*
items.why: *Furniture* is measured, not counted, so it never takes *-s* even though chairs can be counted.

items.prompt: Which is right? *a large number of complaints* or *a large amount of complaints*?
items.why: You can say *two complaints*, so the noun is counted, and counted nouns take *number*.

articles.title: Making a noun mean more than one

article_json.one_line: This gives you every way English turns one thing into more than one, including the endings that change and the nouns that do not change at all.
article_json.short_answer: Add *-s*. After a hissing sound add *-es*: *watches*. After a consonant and *y*, write *-ies*: *studies*. The rest are a short list to learn.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I write the *more than one* form of this word?

body.text: The spelling rules, and the nouns that ignore them

Most nouns add *-s* and nothing else happens. Five spelling rules cover the rest, and two of them exist because of sound rather than spelling. Everything outside those five is a list, and the list is below.

body.caption: Five spelling rules cover every regular plural in English.
body.form_line: the singular noun + *-s*, with five spelling changes

cells: bus → buses; class → classes; branch → branches; box → boxes
study → studies; city → cities; policy → policies
survey → surveys; delay → delays; key → keys
leaf → leaves; knife → knives; half → halves; shelf → shelves
roof → roofs; belief → beliefs; chief → chiefs; cliff → cliffs
*-s* or *-es*, and it is not predictable
photos, pianos, kilos, studios; potatoes, tomatoes, heroes, echoes
both accepted: volcanoes / volcanos; mosquitoes / mosquitos

sub_tables.caption: These change shape instead of adding an ending. There are not many.
These look the same whether there is one or a hundred.
Academic writing runs on these, and the singular is the half people forget.
rows: a section heading in a report

gaps.note: There is no rule. Which nouns take *-es* has to be learnt, so the common ones are listed in the cell instead.

examples.text: Both cities cut their bus services in the same year.
examples.gloss: Two places reduced how often the buses run.

examples.text: The council reviewed its funding criteria in March.
examples.gloss: It looked again at the standards it uses to decide.

examples.text: Twelve species of bird now nest on the reserve.
examples.gloss: Twelve different sorts of bird breed there.

examples.text: Two of the knives were missing from the kitchen.
The team collected three analyses of the same water sample.
examples.gloss: The sample was tested three separate times.

examples.text: Most of the children walk to school along the towpath.
examples.gloss: They go on foot, next to the canal.

notes: *Criteria* and *phenomena* are the more-than-one forms. One of them is *a criterion* and *a phenomenon*.
*People* is the everyday plural of *person*. *Persons* survives only in legal and official notices.
*Fishes* exists and means different species of fish, not more fish.

body.text: Nouns that only ever come in the plural shape
A small group of nouns has no singular at all. They take *are* rather than *is*, and you cannot put *a* in front of them. To count them, English uses *a pair of* or *a set of*.

body.caption: No singular, always *are*, counted with *a pair of* or *a set of*.
rows: the scissors are in the drawer
her savings are in a fixed account
footnotes: *Goods*, *earnings*, *clothes* and *thanks* behave the same way.
A dash means the noun has no counting phrase in normal use.

body.lead_in: Only the noun changes. Watch the verb stay plural every time.

items.text: The premises are closed until the survey is complete.
items.gloss: Nobody can go into the building for now.

items.text: Her savings were wiped out by two years of repairs.
items.gloss: The repairs cost her everything she had put aside.

items.text: I've left the scissors on the shelf by the door.
items.gloss: You will find them on that shelf.

body.so_what: None of these has a singular form, so the verb after them is always plural.

body.headline: Add *-s*. Five spelling rules and three short lists cover the rest.

articles.title: Saying that something belongs to something

article_json.one_line: This gives you the two ways English shows that one thing belongs to another, and tells you which one this sentence needs.
article_json.short_answer: For people and organisations use *'s*: *the council's decision*. For things use *of*: *the cost of the scheme*. Plural already ending in *-s* takes only an apostrophe.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: Do I write *the council's plan* or *the plan of the council*?

body.text: Two ways to say the same thing, and they are not equal

English has two ways to link an owner to what it owns. One puts the owner first with an apostrophe. The other puts the thing first and joins the owner on with *of*. Both are correct, and each sounds right in different places.

body.gloss: the form that says something belongs to somebody: *the council's*, *my*

show_first.text: The council's decision was published on Friday.
My supervisor's comments arrived a week late.
The students' union voted against the fee.

body.anchor_line: The apostrophe is doing the work of a whole phrase. *The council's decision* is a shorter way of saying *the decision belonging to the council*.

body.text: Where the apostrophe goes

body.caption: Look at the owner word first. Its ending decides the apostrophe.
footnotes: The rule is about the owner word, never about the thing owned.

body.lead_in: One owner or several. Only the apostrophe moves.

items.text: The driver's account of the collision was recorded.
items.gloss: One driver said what happened.

items.text: The drivers' accounts of the collision were recorded.
items.gloss: Several drivers each said what happened.

items.text: The women's changing rooms reopened in April.
items.gloss: The rooms for women are usable again.

items.text: I borrowed my sister's bike for the week.
items.gloss: The bike belongs to my sister and I am using it.

body.so_what: The apostrophe sits after the owner word. Where it sits tells the reader whether there is one owner or several.

body.text: Which of the two forms this sentence wants

body.question: Is the owner alive, or an organisation of people?

options.label: *'s*
options.use_it_when: The owner is a person, an animal, a group of people, a country, or a length of time.
options.example: The committee's report runs to ninety pages.

options.label: *of*
options.use_it_when: The owner is a thing or an idea, or the owner phrase is long.
options.example: The cost of the flood defences has doubled.

a.text: The surveyor's report arrived on Thursday.
a.means: A person wrote it, and she is the one you are pointing at.

b.text: The report of the survey arrived on Thursday.
b.means: The report came out of a piece of work, not out of a named person.

a.text: The town's population fell by four per cent.
a.means: You are treating the town as a body of people.

b.text: The population of the town fell by four per cent.
b.means: The same fact, written in the flatter form a report would use.

a.text: The roof of the sports hall leaks in two places.
a.means: The building has a leaking roof.
a.span: The roof of the sports hall

b.text: The sports hall's roof leaks in two places.
b.means: The same fact, and it sounds ordinary rather than formal.

minimal_pairs.only_difference: of the sports hall / sports hall's

a.text: She gave two weeks' notice before leaving.
a.means: She told them two weeks before her last day.

b.text: She gave notice two weeks before leaving.
b.means: The same fact, with the time as an ordinary time phrase.

minimal_pairs.only_difference: two weeks' notice / notice two weeks

body.deciding_factor: If the owner could sign its name, use *'s*. If it could not, use *of*, unless *'s* sounds ordinary to you.
body.trap: You were taught that *'s* is for people and *of* is for things, so you avoid *'s* with anything that is not a human being. Towns, companies, committees and lengths of time all take *'s* freely.
body.register_note: *Of* is the flatter, more formal choice and it carries most academic writing. *'s* is shorter and it is what speech uses. Both belong in Task 2.

body.text: The two forms overlap widely, so most of the time either is correct. The one place the choice is forced is length: a long owner phrase goes after *of*, because a reader cannot hold six words and then meet an apostrophe.
Use *'s* when the owner is a person, a group or a length of time. Use *of* when the owner phrase is long.

body.lead_in: The owner phrase gets longer each time. Watch where it has to move.

items.text: The tenant's letter was passed to the housing office.
items.gloss: One tenant wrote in and the letter was sent on.

items.text: The letter of the tenant who reported the damp was passed on.
items.gloss: The person who wrote it is identified by what she did.

marks.span: of the tenant who reported the damp

items.text: Next year's budget has already been agreed.
items.gloss: The money for the coming year is settled.

items.text: That's my flatmate's laptop, not mine.
items.gloss: The laptop belongs to the person I live with.

body.so_what: As the owner phrase grows, the apostrophe stops working and *of* takes over.

body.text: *A friend of mine*, and why *a friend of me* is wrong
When you want to say *one of the ones belonging to me*, English uses *of* plus the possessive form, not the object form. So it is *a friend of mine* and *a colleague of my sister's*.

body.lead_in: Only the word after *of* changes, and only one version is English.

items.text: A colleague of mine reviewed the drainage plan.
items.gloss: Somebody I work with looked at the plan.

items.text: Two neighbours of ours objected to the extension.
items.gloss: Two people who live near us wrote in against it.

items.text: That old photograph of my grandmother's is in the hall.
items.gloss: The photograph belongs to my grandmother.

body.so_what: The word after *of* is always the belonging form: *mine*, *ours*, *theirs*, or a noun with *'s*.

body.text: What goes wrong with the apostrophe

body.wrong: The tenant's on the third floor all reported the same fault.
body.right: The tenants on the third floor all reported the same fault.
body.why_it_happens: The word ends in *-s* and an apostrophe often goes with *-s*, so the two get joined. An apostrophe never makes a plural. It only ever marks belonging or a missing letter.
body.smallest_fix: Ask whether anything belongs to the tenants. If not, delete the apostrophe.

body.wrong: The scheme lost it's funding halfway through the year.
body.right: The scheme lost its funding halfway through the year.
body.why_it_happens: Every other belonging form takes an apostrophe, so *its* looks as though it should too. *It's* is already taken: it is the short form of *it is* and *it has*.
body.smallest_fix: Read it aloud as *it is*. If that makes no sense, write *its* with no apostrophe.

body.wrong: A friend of me works at the recycling centre.
body.right: A friend of mine works at the recycling centre.
body.why_it_happens: *Of* is followed by the object form everywhere else, so *me* looks right. In this one pattern *of* is followed by the belonging form instead.
body.smallest_fix: Change *me* to *mine*, *us* to *ours*, *them* to *theirs*.

body.heard: You can only use *'s* with people. Everything else takes *of*.
also_known_as: the apostrophe is for living things
body.truth: Organisations, places, vehicles and lengths of time all take *'s* in ordinary written English: *the government's response*, *the city's transport plan*, *a day's work*, *the train's arrival time*.
body.what_to_do: Use *'s* for people, groups, places and time. Use *of* when the owner is an idea or when the owner phrase is more than about three words long.

body.headline: Look at the owner word. Its ending decides the apostrophe.

articles.title: The word *a* in front of a noun

article_json.one_line: This tells you when a noun needs *a* in front of it, and whether to write *a* or *an* before this particular word.
article_json.short_answer: Use *a* the first time you mention one countable thing. Write *an* only when the next word starts with a vowel sound: *an hour*, *a university*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: When do I put *a* in front of a word, and when is it *an*?

body.text: What *a* tells your reader

*A* means one, and it means the reader does not yet know which one. You are introducing something for the first time. That is why the next sentence can switch to *the*: by then the reader knows which one you mean.

body.lead_in: Watch the same noun come back in the second sentence with a different word in front of it.

items.text: A cycle lane was added last summer.
items.gloss: There is a cycle lane there now, and this is the first you have heard of it.

items.text: The cycle lane has already been resurfaced twice.
items.gloss: The same lane, which you now know about, has been repaired twice.

items.text: She has taken a job at the recycling centre.
items.gloss: She works there now, and you did not know about the job.

items.text: A second survey was commissioned in the same year.
items.gloss: They paid for another survey, and this is its first mention.

body.so_what: *A* opens the door on something new. *The* is what you use once the reader is already inside.

body.text: The four jobs *a* does

body.caption: Four different sentences, one word doing four different things.
headers: What the reader takes from it
rows: a leak was reported on Monday
you have not heard about this leak
she is a governor at the college
a bicycle costs less to run than a car
this is true of bicycles in general
footnotes: The fourth job is the one that surprises people. *A* can make a general statement about a whole kind of thing.

body.text: *A* or *an* is decided by sound, not by spelling
Say the next word out loud. Vowel sound at the start, write *an*. Consonant sound at the start, write *a*.

body.lead_in: Every one of these has a first letter that points the wrong way. Say them and you get the right answer.

items.text: She waited an hour outside the housing office.
items.gloss: She was there for sixty minutes.

items.text: He is applying to a university in the north.
items.gloss: He wants a place there.

items.text: The tenant wrote to an MP about the damp.
items.gloss: She contacted the person who represents her.

items.text: It is a one-way street, so the lorry had to reverse.
items.gloss: Traffic only goes in one direction there.

items.text: The panel gave an honest account of the delay.
items.gloss: They said what really happened.

body.so_what: *Hour* begins with a written *h* and a spoken vowel, so it takes *an*. *University* begins with a written vowel and a spoken *y*, so it takes *a*.

body.caption: The letter at the front lies in both directions.
footnotes: Some older writing uses *an hotel* and *an historic*. Both are dated. *A hotel* and *a historic* are the ordinary forms now.

body.text: Where a singular noun is left bare and should not be

body.wrong: Government should invest more in public transport.
body.right: Governments should invest more in public transport.
body.why_it_happens: You mean governments in general, and a general statement feels as though it needs no word in front of it. English only allows that with plurals and with uncountable nouns, so the singular has to change.
body.smallest_fix: Make the noun plural, or put *the* or *a* in front of it.

body.wrong: The report describes a new measures for reducing waste.
body.right: The report describes new measures for reducing waste.
body.why_it_happens: *A* is the word you reach for when something is new to the reader, and these measures are new. *A* also means one, so it cannot sit in front of a plural noun.
body.smallest_fix: Delete *a* in front of a plural, or make the noun singular.

body.wrong: She is studying for an university degree in engineering.
body.right: She is studying for a university degree in engineering.
body.why_it_happens: *U* is a vowel letter, so *an* looks correct. The choice runs on sound, and *university* starts with the sound of *y*.
body.smallest_fix: Say the word out loud. If it starts with a *y* or *w* sound, use *a*.

body.mechanism: Chinese marks how many with a counting word between the number and the noun, and it has no separate word that means *one of a kind not yet known*.
body.wrong: She is teacher at the college in Norland.
body.right: She is a teacher at the college in Norland.
body.fix: Put *a* in front of a singular job or role, even when the sentence feels complete.

also_known_as: an goes before the five vowel letters
body.truth: That is a rule about letters, and the choice runs on sound. It gets *an hour* wrong, because the *h* is silent, and it gets *a university* wrong, because the *u* is said like *you*.
body.what_to_do: Say the next word out loud and listen to the first sound. Use the letters only when you cannot hear the word in your head.

articles.title: The word *the*, and what it promises the reader

article_json.one_line: This tells you when to put *the* in front of a noun, by asking one question about what your reader already knows.
article_json.short_answer: Use *the* when your reader can tell which one you mean. They can tell if you already mentioned it, if there is only one, or if the words after it say which.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I know whether this noun needs *the*?

body.text: *The* is a promise that your reader can identify it

*The* does not mean the noun is important, and it does not mean the noun is specific in your head. It means the reader can work out which one you mean. If they cannot, *the* leaves them looking for something they have never been shown.
So the question is never about the thing. It is about the reader. Ask yourself: could they point at it?

body.lead_in: Every one of these uses *the*, and in each one the reader can point at what it means.
body.dimension: why the reader can identify it

items.text: The lift has been out of order since Tuesday.
items.gloss: There is one lift in this building, and we both know it.

items.text: The cost of the repairs came to nine thousand pounds.
items.gloss: The repairs we are discussing cost that much.

items.text: The government withdrew the funding in October.
items.gloss: The country's government stopped paying.

items.text: The first stage of the scheme finished ahead of time.
items.gloss: Stage one was done early.

body.so_what: In each one you could ask *which one?* and the answer is already on the page or in the room.

body.text: The four reasons a reader can identify it

body.caption: Four different ways the reader gets told which one.
rows: a leak appeared. the leak spread.
you told them in the last sentence
the sun, the internet, the coast
there is nothing else it could be
the kitchen, the manager, the deadline
one per building, per office, per task
the words after it say which
*of the repairs* narrows it to one
it is the top or the first
the highest figure, the second stage
only one thing can be highest
footnotes: *Same*, *only*, *next*, *last* and *right* behave like the top-or-first row: *the same result*, *the only option*.

body.text: Use *the* when your reader can already tell which one you mean, whether from your last sentence, from the situation, or from the words that follow.

body.lead_in: The words after the noun are what makes it identifiable each time.

items.text: The report I sent you on Friday has been withdrawn.
items.gloss: One particular report is no longer valid, and you know which.

marks.span: The report I sent you on Friday

items.text: The rise in energy prices hit rural households hardest.
items.gloss: Energy prices went up and it was worse for people in the country.

items.text: The bus that stops outside the library runs every ten minutes.
items.gloss: One particular bus is frequent.

marks.span: The bus that stops outside the library

items.text: The effect on local shops was immediate.
items.gloss: Shops nearby felt it straight away.

body.so_what: *Of*, *in*, *on* and a *that*-clause after the noun all do the same job: they tell the reader which one, so *the* becomes correct.

body.text: *The* with superlatives, ordinals and groups of people

Three patterns take *the* automatically, because in each of them only one answer is possible. Nothing else can be the highest, nothing else can be second, and there is only one group of unemployed people in the country you are writing about.

body.caption: In each of these there is only one possible answer, so *the* is fixed.
rows: the largest employer in the district
the first, the third, the last
the second stage began in May
footnotes: *The* is dropped after a belonging word: *her best result*, not *her the best result*.

body.label: Four sorts of name that keep *the*, and this is the whole list

items.text: Rivers, seas, oceans, deserts, canals and mountain ranges.
items.example: The canal was drained for two weeks in February.

items.text: Country names that are plural or that contain an ordinary noun.
items.example: The Netherlands has one of the densest cycle networks in Europe.

items.text: Newspapers, hotels, cinemas, museums and theatres.
items.example: The Marlow Museum opens at ten on weekdays.

items.text: Organisations named with *of*, and most named with initials read as words.
items.example: The University of Sandmouth published the figures last month.

body.stop_line: That is the whole list for names. Every other town, country, street, person and single mountain takes no word in front of it.

body.text: What goes wrong once *the* has been learnt

body.wrong: The technology has changed the way the people work.
body.right: Technology has changed the way people work.
body.why_it_happens: You are making a big claim, and a big claim feels as though it deserves a strong word in front of the noun. *The* narrows things down instead, so it turns a statement about everybody into a statement about one particular group.
body.smallest_fix: Take *the* out of any noun that means the whole kind rather than a particular set.

body.wrong: Cost of the new footbridge rose by a third.
body.right: The cost of the new footbridge rose by a third.
body.why_it_happens: The sentence starts with the noun, and a sentence-opening noun often needs no word in front of it. *Of the new footbridge* has already told the reader which cost, so *the* is required.
body.smallest_fix: If an *of*-phrase follows the noun, put *the* in front of it.

body.wrong: I want to describe the problem that many cities now face.
body.right: I want to describe a problem that many cities now face.
body.why_it_happens: You know exactly which problem you mean, so *the* feels right. Your reader has not met it yet, so the first mention needs *a*.
body.smallest_fix: Ask whether the reader has met this thing. If not, use *a* and switch to *the* afterwards.

body.heard: Use *the* when you are talking about something specific.
body.truth: You always have something specific in mind, so that rule says use *the* every time. The test is whether your **reader** can tell which one. *I bought a laptop* is about one specific laptop, and it still takes *a*.
body.what_to_do: Ask *can my reader point at it?* rather than *do I mean a particular one?* If they cannot point at it yet, use *a* or no word at all.

body.headline: *The* means your reader can already tell which one.

items.why: *Of applicants* tells the reader which number, so the noun is identified and takes *the*.

items.prompt: Why is *The pollution is a problem in the big cities* usually wrong?
items.answer: Both nouns are meant in general, so neither takes *the*: *Pollution is a problem in big cities.*
items.why: *The* narrows a noun down to a particular set, and a general claim is about all of them.

articles.title: When a noun needs nothing in front of it

article_json.also_called: No article, and how English makes a generalisation
article_json.one_line: This tells you when a noun stands on its own, which is what a general statement in an essay almost always needs.
article_json.short_answer: To talk about something in general, use a plural or an uncountable noun with nothing in front of it: *Electric cars are expensive.* *Research takes time.*
article_json.question_in_learner_words: When do I leave the noun with no word in front of it?

body.text: A general statement takes a bare noun

Most sentences in an essay are about a whole kind of thing, not about a particular set of them. English writes those with nothing in front of the noun. Adding *the* points at a particular group instead, and that changes the claim.

body.lead_in: Nothing sits in front of these nouns, and each sentence is about the whole kind.

items.text: Electric vehicles are still expensive to insure.
items.gloss: Insurance costs more for electric cars than for other cars.

items.text: Renewable energy is getting cheaper every year.
items.gloss: The price of power from wind and sun keeps falling.

items.text: Governments rarely fund research that takes twenty years.
items.gloss: Long projects find it hard to get public money.

items.text: Traffic gets worse every time they close the bypass.
items.gloss: Closing that road makes the jams worse.

body.so_what: Each sentence is about the whole kind of thing, and none of them has a word in front of the noun.

body.text: To talk about a whole kind of thing, use a plural noun or an uncountable noun, with nothing in front of it.

body.lead_in: Only the word in front of the noun changes, and the claim changes with it.

items.text: Cyclists are more exposed to air pollution than drivers.
items.gloss: This is true of cyclists as a whole.

items.text: The cyclists were held up for an hour at the junction.
items.gloss: One particular group of cyclists was delayed.

items.text: Public transport works best when it runs late at night.
items.gloss: Buses and trains in general are more useful with late services.

items.text: The public transport in Sandmouth stops at half past ten.
items.gloss: One town's buses and trains finish early.

body.so_what: *The* narrowed each sentence down from everybody to one particular set.

body.text: Three ways to say something in general, and what each sounds like
English has three patterns for a general claim, and they are not interchangeable. The bare plural is the one an essay wants. The other two carry a flavour, so use them on purpose.

body.caption: Three ways to generalise, and the bare plural is the safe one.
rows: neutral, and right in almost any essay
electric vehicles cost more to insure
any typical one, good for a definition
an electric vehicle costs more to insure
formal or technical, the thing as an invention
the bicycle changed how cities grew
footnotes: *The* + plural is not on this list, because it is not a generalisation. It points at a particular set.

body.lead_in: The same claim in three patterns. Watch the flavour change, not the fact.

items.text: Heat pumps cost less to run than gas boilers.
items.gloss: Running a heat pump is cheaper.

items.text: A heat pump costs less to run than a gas boiler.
items.gloss: The same fact, stated about one typical example of each.

items.text: The heat pump has changed how new houses are heated.
items.gloss: The invention itself changed building practice.

items.text: Heat pumps are noisy, though, aren't they?
items.gloss: You are asking whether that is generally true of them.

body.so_what: All four are correct. The bare plural is the one that never sounds odd, which is why it carries an essay.

body.text: The fixed phrases that take no word in front

body.caption: In each pair, the bare noun means the purpose and *the* means the building.
rows: the lunch they served was cold
by train, by bus, on foot
at university, in prison, at work, in bed
the university has a new library
in March, on Friday, in 2019, at night
footnotes: The purpose row is the one that carries meaning. *In hospital* means as a patient; *in the hospital* means inside the building.

body.text: What goes wrong when the bare noun is skipped

body.wrong: In the modern society, the technology changes very fast.
body.right: In modern society, technology changes very fast.
body.why_it_happens: The opening of an essay feels formal, and *the* feels like the formal choice. Both nouns here mean the whole kind, so both need to stand bare.
body.smallest_fix: Delete *the* in front of any noun that means the whole kind of thing.

body.wrong: The young people today spend too long on their phones.
body.right: Young people today spend too long on their phones.
body.why_it_happens: You mean all of them, and *the* feels as though it makes the group complete. *The* + a plural noun points at one particular set of people, so it shrinks the claim rather than widening it.
body.smallest_fix: Delete *the*. Keep it only if you have already named which group you mean.

body.wrong: Student needs somewhere quiet to work in the evening.
body.right: Students need somewhere quiet to work in the evening.
body.why_it_happens: Bare nouns are correct for general statements, so a singular one looks correct too. Only plural and uncountable nouns can stand bare, so a singular one has to change or take a word in front.
body.smallest_fix: Make the noun plural, or write *a student needs*.

body.mechanism: Arabic marks a general statement with the definite marker on the noun, so the general form and the identified form look alike.
body.wrong: The pollution is a serious problem in the cities.
body.right: Pollution is a serious problem in cities.
body.fix: For a claim about the whole kind, take the word in front of the noun away.

body.heard: Every noun needs a word in front of it.
also_known_as: never start a sentence with a bare noun
body.truth: That is true only of singular countable nouns. Plural nouns and uncountable nouns stand bare whenever the claim is general, and in an essay that is most sentences.
body.what_to_do: Check the noun first. Singular and countable, it needs something. Plural or uncountable, leave it bare unless the reader needs to know which ones.

articles.title: Which little word goes in front of this noun?

article_json.one_line: This gives you a three-question procedure you can run inside a sentence, instead of a rule list you have to remember all of.
article_json.short_answer: Ask three things, in order. General claim? Nothing. Reader knows which one? *The*. Otherwise, singular countable? *A*. That covers most sentences.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: I am halfway through a sentence. Do I write *a*, *the*, or nothing?

body.text: Why a list of rules does not help mid-sentence

You already know the rules. The trouble is that you are writing, and a list of fourteen rules cannot be checked in the second and a half you have. What works is a short procedure that always runs in the same order.
Three questions do most of the work. Run them in order and stop at the first one that answers. The rest of the article is those three questions, and what to do when none of them fires.

body.question: Can my reader already tell which one I mean?

options.label: nothing
options.use_it_when: The noun is plural or uncountable, and you mean the whole kind rather than a particular set.
options.example: Rural bus services have been cut in most counties.

options.label: *the*
options.use_it_when: The reader can point at it: you mentioned it, there is only one, or the words after it say which.
options.example: The bus service to Marlow was cut in April.

options.label: *a* / *an*
options.use_it_when: The noun is singular and countable, and the reader has not met this one yet.
options.example: A bus service was withdrawn without any consultation.

a.text: Libraries are closing across the county.
a.means: Libraries in general are shutting. You are making a claim about all of them.

b.text: The libraries are closing across the county.
b.means: A particular set of libraries that you have already named is shutting.

a.text: She has taken a laptop from the store cupboard.
a.means: She took one of the laptops. You are not saying which.

b.text: She has taken the laptop from the store cupboard.
b.means: She took the one particular laptop we both know about.

a.text: He went to school in Norland until he was sixteen.
a.means: He was a pupil there. You are talking about his education.

b.text: He went to the school in Norland to collect a form.
b.means: He walked to the building for another reason entirely.

a.text: Water is charged by the cubic metre in this district.
a.means: Water in general is billed that way here.

b.text: The water in the storage tank has not been tested.
b.means: One particular quantity of water has not been checked.

body.deciding_factor: Ask what your reader knows, not what you know. If they cannot point at it, *the* is wrong.
body.trap: You were taught that *the* is for specific things, and you always have a specific thing in mind, so *the* creeps into every noun. The test is about the reader, not about you.
body.register_note: The same procedure runs in speech and in writing. It pays hardest in Task 2, where a single wrong *the* turns a claim about everybody into a claim about one group.

body.intro: Three questions, in this order. Stop at the first one that answers.

steps.ask: Is the noun plural or uncountable, and do you mean the whole kind?

verdict.example: Rural bus services have been cut in most counties.
verdict.why: A claim about the whole kind takes a bare plural or a bare uncountable noun.

branches.answer: No, or the noun is singular

steps.ask: Can your reader already tell which one you mean?

branches.answer: Yes — mentioned, unique, or named by the words after it

verdict.example: The bus service to Marlow was cut in April.
verdict.why: *The* is a promise that the reader can identify it, and here they can.

branches.answer: No — this is new to them

steps.ask: Is the noun singular and countable?

verdict.example: A bus service was withdrawn without any consultation.
verdict.why: A singular countable noun is never left bare, and the reader has not met this one.

branches.answer: No — it is plural or uncountable

verdict.example: The depot has taken delivery of new equipment.
verdict.why: Plural and uncountable nouns can stand bare, and *some* adds a vague amount.

body.text: Most sentences stop at the first or the second question. The third only runs when the noun is new to the reader, which is why the commonest error is a *the* that should have been an *a*.
The three rules underneath the procedure

body.lead_in: Three statements carry most of the article system:
items: A singular countable noun is never bare. It takes *a*, *the*, *this*, *my*, *each* or something.
A general claim takes a bare plural or a bare uncountable noun.
*The* goes on once the thing has been identified, by earlier mention, by uniqueness, or by the words that follow.

body.caption: The same noun, run through the procedure four times.
footnotes: Row three follows row two in a real paragraph. That switch from *a* to *the* is the commonest article move in English.

body.lead_in: One short paragraph. Watch the word in front of *scheme* change as the reader learns about it.

items.text: Councils across the region have tried car-free schemes.
items.gloss: This sort of scheme has been tried in lots of places.

items.text: Sandmouth launched a scheme of this kind in 2021.
items.gloss: One town started one, and this is its first mention.

items.text: The scheme cut traffic in the centre by a fifth.
items.gloss: That same scheme reduced the traffic.

items.text: So the scheme worked, and nobody expected that.
items.gloss: It succeeded, which was a surprise.

body.so_what: Nothing about the scheme changed. What changed is how much the reader had been told.

body.text: What goes wrong when the procedure is skipped

body.wrong: The children who grow up near a main road have more asthma.
body.right: Children who grow up near a main road have more asthma.
body.why_it_happens: The words after the noun look as though they identify which children, so *the* feels earned. Here they describe a kind of child rather than pointing at a known group, so the claim is general and the noun stands bare.
body.smallest_fix: Ask whether you mean all of them or a known set. All of them, delete *the*.

body.wrong: Results of the second trial were published in June.
body.right: The results of the second trial were published in June.
body.why_it_happens: You have been told that general statements take a bare noun, and this looks like one. *Of the second trial* names which results, so the reader can identify them and *the* is required.
body.smallest_fix: If an *of*-phrase or a *that*-clause follows the noun, put *the* in front.

body.wrong: Solution to this problem will take several years.
body.right: A solution to this problem will take several years.
body.why_it_happens: The sentence opens on the noun, and opening nouns often stand bare. *Solution* is singular and countable, and English never leaves that bare.
body.smallest_fix: Put *a* in front, or make the noun plural.

body.what_varies: Whether *the* appears in front of an institution named by its purpose.

option_a.label: British English
option_a.example: She spent three days in hospital after the fall.

option_b.label: American English
option_b.example: She spent three days in the hospital after the fall.

body.why_this_default: Our examples use British conventions throughout. Both forms are standard, and neither is an error. This is a house choice, not a rule of English.

body.heard: Use *a* the first time and *the* every time after that.
also_known_as: first mention a, second mention the
body.truth: That half works, and it is the reason for a whole class of errors. It says nothing about the general claims that fill an essay, where the correct answer is nothing at all, and nothing about the *the* that comes from an *of*-phrase on a first mention.
body.what_to_do: Run the general-claim question first, before you think about first or second mention. *Governments should act* has no first mention and no word in front of it.

articles.title: Pointing at things, and saying whose they are

article_json.one_line: This gives you the words that point at a thing and the words that say who it belongs to, and shows why they cannot stack.
article_json.short_answer: *This* and *these* are near or just mentioned. *That* and *those* are further off. *My*, *your*, *their* say whose, and they replace *the*, never join it.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: When do I write *this* and when *that*, and can I say *the my house*?

body.text: Words that point, and words that say whose

Two small families of words go in the same slot as *a* and *the*. One family points at something. The other says who it belongs to. They fill the same slot, so only one of them can be there at a time.

body.caption: Near or far, one or several: four words cover the whole grid.
footnotes: Distance can be in space, in time, or in the text. *This morning* is now; *that morning* was some time ago.

body.caption: One word per owner, and none of them changes for a plural noun.
footnotes: *Its* has no apostrophe. *It's* is the short form of *it is*.
These words never take *-s* and never change for a plural noun after them.

body.lead_in: Only the pointing word changes. Watch the distance move.

items.text: This bus goes to the station; that one does not.
items.gloss: The bus in front of us is the right one.

items.text: These figures come from the 2019 survey.
items.gloss: The numbers you are looking at now come from that survey.

items.text: Those delays were caused by a burst water main.
items.gloss: The delays we talked about earlier had that cause.

items.text: Her application arrived before the deadline.
items.gloss: The application belonging to her was on time.

body.so_what: *This* and *these* pull the thing close. *That* and *those* push it away, in space or in time.

body.text: One slot, one word: they cannot stack
Only one of *a*, *the*, *this*, *that*, *my* or *your* goes in front of a noun. They fill the same slot, so they never appear together.

body.lead_in: One word in the slot each time, and each one gives the reader something different.

items.text: A survey found damp in nineteen flats.
items.gloss: Some survey found it, and you have not met the survey before.

items.text: The survey found damp in nineteen flats.
items.gloss: The survey we already know about found it.

items.text: This survey found damp in nineteen flats.
items.gloss: The one in front of you, or the one just named, found it.

items.text: Our survey found damp in nineteen flats.
items.gloss: The one we carried out found it.

body.so_what: The slot in front of the noun holds exactly one word, and which word you choose is what the reader reads.

body.text: To say both *whose* and *which one*, English uses *of* instead of stacking. So *a friend of mine* does the job of *a my friend*, and *that car of theirs* does the job of *that their car*.
*This* in writing, where the distance is in the text

In an essay, *this* usually points back at your own last sentence rather than at anything in the room. It works best with a noun after it, because a bare *this* leaves the reader guessing what you mean.

body.lead_in: Only the noun after *this* changes, and the reader gets more each time.

items.text: This has caused problems for rural households.
items.gloss: Something in the last sentence caused problems, and the reader has to guess which part.

items.text: This shift has caused problems for rural households.
items.gloss: The change you just described is what caused them.

items.text: This funding cut has caused problems for rural households.
items.gloss: The cut in money you just described is the cause.

items.text: That's the bit I don't follow, to be honest.
items.gloss: You are pointing at something the other person just said.

body.so_what: A noun after *this* tells the reader exactly which part of your last sentence you mean.

body.text: What goes wrong in the slot

body.wrong: The my colleague sent the figures on Tuesday.
body.right: My colleague sent the figures on Tuesday.
body.why_it_happens: You know exactly which colleague, so *the* feels needed as well. *My* already tells the reader which one, so the two words are competing for one slot.
body.smallest_fix: Delete *the*. A word like *my* or *this* does the identifying on its own.

body.wrong: This findings suggest that the scheme had little effect.
body.right: These findings suggest that the scheme had little effect.
body.why_it_happens: The set of findings feels like one thing, so the singular word comes out. *This* and *that* only go with one thing; more than one takes *these* and *those*.
body.smallest_fix: Count the noun. Plural noun, use *these* or *those*.

body.wrong: The tutor marked the essay and gave his feedback on Friday.
body.right: The tutor marked the essay and gave her feedback on Friday.
body.why_it_happens: In many languages the belonging word matches the thing owned, not the owner. In English it matches the owner, so *feedback* has no say in the choice.
body.smallest_fix: Look at the owner, not at the thing owned, and pick *his*, *her*, *its* or *their*.

body.mechanism: Spanish matches the belonging word to the thing owned, so one form covers both a male and a female owner.
body.wrong: My sister sent his notes from the seminar.
body.right: My sister sent her notes from the seminar.
body.fix: Choose the word by looking at who owns it, not at what is owned.

body.heard: *This* is for things that are physically close and *that* is for things far away.
also_known_as: this means here and that means there
body.truth: Distance is only one of the three things these words measure. In writing they mark distance in the text, and in speech they often mark distance in time: *this week* is the one we are in, *that week* is one we have left behind.
body.what_to_do: Ask whether the thing is current or already behind you. Current takes *this*; finished or earlier takes *that*.

body.text: The noun picks the word, not the other way round
Every word for amount belongs to one of three groups: countable nouns only, uncountable nouns only, or both. So the decision starts with the noun. Count it, then pick from the right column.

show_first.text: Many households were affected by the closure.
There isn't much evidence for that claim.
A few colleges have already adopted the scheme.

body.name_line: A word like that is called a **quantifier**.
body.anchor_line: It sits in the same place as *the* and *a*, and it answers a different question: not which one, but how many or how much.

body.caption: Count the noun, then read down the column it belongs to.
footnotes: *A lot of*, *plenty of* and *some* go with both, which makes them the safe choice when you are unsure.

body.lead_in: Only the noun changes. Watch the word in front of it change with it.

items.gloss: A lot of homes changed who supplied their energy.

body.so_what: *Many* went with a noun you can count, *much* with one you measure, and *plenty of* with either.

body.text: *Much* is awkward in a plain positive sentence
*Much* is normal in negatives, in questions, and after *so*, *too*, *as* and *how*. In a plain positive statement it sounds stiff and old, so a formal phrase does the job instead.

rows: a great deal of research supports this
there isn't much research on this
footnotes: The same split does not affect *many*, which is fine in positives, negatives and questions alike.

body.text: *Some* and *any*, and the offer that breaks the pattern
Use *some* in positive statements and in offers and requests. Use *any* in negatives, in most questions, and to mean *it does not matter which*.

body.lead_in: Only *some* or *any* changes, and what the sentence is doing changes with it.

items.gloss: You are offering, and you expect the answer to be yes.

items.text: Any student on the course can borrow the equipment.
items.gloss: It does not matter which student. All of them can.

body.so_what: *Some* in a question is an offer. *Any* in a positive sentence means it does not matter which one.

body.text: *A few* and *few* mean opposite things

This is the one place where a single letter reverses the point of a sentence. With *a*, you are saying there are some, and that is good news. Without it, you are saying there are hardly any, and that is the complaint.

body.caption: With *a*, some and positive. Without *a*, hardly any and negative.
rows: a few colleges have adopted it
hardly any, and that is the problem
hardly any, and that is the problem
footnotes: Bare *few* and *little* are formal. In speech people say *not many* and *not much* instead.

body.lead_in: The only change is the word *a*, and the conclusion flips each time.

items.text: A few residents objected to the parking scheme.
items.gloss: Some people complained, so there was opposition.

items.text: Few residents objected to the parking scheme.
items.gloss: Almost nobody complained, so the scheme went ahead easily.

items.text: There is a little support for a night bus service.
items.gloss: Some people want one, so the idea is alive.

items.text: There is little support for a night bus service.
items.gloss: Almost nobody wants one, so it will not happen.

body.so_what: One letter, and the reader draws the opposite conclusion. This one is worth reading twice.

body.text: What goes wrong with words for amount

body.wrong: The study drew on many research from three universities.
body.right: The study drew on a great deal of research from three universities.
body.why_it_happens: *Research* arrives in separate studies, so it feels countable, and *many* is the word for a lot of countable things. English measures research rather than counting it.
body.smallest_fix: Change *many* to *a great deal of* or *a lot of*, and leave the noun singular.

body.wrong: The office doesn't have some spare keys for the side door.
body.right: The office doesn't have any spare keys for the side door.
body.why_it_happens: You have been told that *some* is used for offers and requests, and this feels like a polite sentence. That exception covers questions, not negatives, so a negative takes *any*.
body.smallest_fix: In a sentence with *not* in it, change *some* to *any*.

body.wrong: Few of my classmates helped me, so the work was finished quickly.
body.right: A few of my classmates helped me, so the work was finished quickly.
body.why_it_happens: Both forms mean a small number, so they look interchangeable. Bare *few* is a complaint, and it contradicts the second half of this sentence.
body.smallest_fix: If the small number is good news, put *a* in front.

body.heard: Use *any* in questions and *some* in statements.
also_known_as: some for positive, any for question
body.truth: That half works. *Some* is normal in a question when you are offering or requesting, because you expect the answer to be yes: *Would you like some tea?* And *any* is normal in a statement when it means *it does not matter which*: *Any bus will get you there.*
body.what_to_do: Ask what the sentence is doing. Offering or requesting takes *some*, whatever the punctuation. Meaning *whichever* takes *any*, even in a statement.

body.text: Same group, four ways of looking at it
*All*, *every*, *each* and *both* can describe the same set of people. They differ in whether you are seeing the group together or one member at a time, and that difference decides the verb.

body.caption: Together takes a plural verb. One at a time takes a singular one.
rows: one at a time, small set
either noun, verb follows the noun
footnotes: *Every* means all of them and still takes a singular verb. That mismatch is the commonest trap in this group.

body.lead_in: Same fact each time. Only the word for the group changes, and the verb follows it.

items.text: All the rooms were checked before the inspection.
items.gloss: The checking got done, and you are treating it as one job.

items.text: Each room was checked before the inspection.
items.gloss: The rooms were checked one by one, and that is the point.

body.so_what: *All* and *both* see the group together and take a plural verb. *Every* and *each* see it one at a time and take a singular one.

body.text: When these words need *of*, and when they must not have it
The word *of* is not decoration. It appears when the noun already has *the*, *these*, *my* or a pronoun after it, and it stays away when the noun is bare.
Add *of* when a word like *the*, *these*, *my* or a pronoun comes next. Leave *of* out when the noun stands bare.

body.lead_in: The same word each time. Only what follows it decides whether *of* appears.

items.text: Most students take the bus rather than drive.
items.gloss: You are talking about students in general.

items.text: Most of the students on this course take the bus.
items.gloss: You are talking about one particular group of students.

items.text: All applicants must supply two references.
items.gloss: The rule covers everybody who applies.

items.text: All of them missed the deadline by a week.
items.gloss: Every person in the group we were discussing was late.

body.so_what: *Of* turns a claim about everybody into a claim about one named group. It is never optional decoration.

body.caption: Bare noun, no *of*. A word like *the* after it, *of* is required.
rows: all of the students, all the students
both of the proposals, both the proposals
footnotes: *All* and *both* may drop the *of* in front of *the*: *all the students* and *all of the students* are both correct.
A dash means the pattern does not exist. *Every* cannot take *of*, and *none* cannot stand in front of a bare noun.

body.text: The order these little words go in
Three of these words can sit in front of *the* rather than instead of it. That gives a fixed order, and it is the reason a phrase like *the all reasons* sounds wrong.

body.caption: Front slot, middle slot, number slot, then the noun.
footnotes: A dash means the slot is empty in that row. Every slot is optional; the order is not.
*Such*, *what*, *quite* and *rather* go in the front slot and push *a* to the right: *such a delay*, *quite a change*, *rather a shame*.

body.lead_in: Words are added one slot at a time, and none of them moves.

items.text: The reasons for the delay were never made public.
items.gloss: Nobody explained why it was late.

items.text: All the reasons for the delay were never made public.
items.gloss: Not one of the reasons was explained.

items.text: All the many reasons for the delay were listed in the appendix.
items.gloss: There were a lot of reasons and every one was written down.

items.text: It was such a delay that half the audience left.
items.gloss: The wait was so long that many people gave up.

body.so_what: The slots fill from the left. Nothing ever moves in front of *all*, and nothing ever squeezes between *the* and the number.

body.text: What goes wrong with the whole-group words

body.wrong: Every students on the course have to register by Friday.
body.right: Every student on the course has to register by Friday.
body.why_it_happens: *Every* means all of them, so a plural noun and a plural verb feel right. *Every* looks at them one at a time, so the noun and the verb both stay singular.
body.smallest_fix: Drop the *-s* from the noun and match the verb to it.

body.wrong: Most of students in the survey cycled to work at least once.
body.right: Most of the students in the survey cycled to work at least once.
body.why_it_happens: *Most of* is a fixed phrase in your ear, so it gets used in front of a bare noun. *Of* needs a word like *the* or *these* after it, so either add one or take *of* out.
body.smallest_fix: Write *most students* or *most of the students*. Never *most of students*.

body.wrong: All of applicants were interviewed within two weeks.
body.right: All applicants were interviewed within two weeks.
body.why_it_happens: The same fixed phrase problem as *most of*. *All* goes straight in front of a bare noun, and *of* is only for when a word like *the* follows.
body.smallest_fix: Delete *of*, or write *all of the applicants*.

body.label: Three agreement points where careful writing and speech differ

items.text: *Neither of* and *either of* take a singular verb in careful writing. A plural verb after them is very common in speech.
items.example: Neither of the reports is complete.

items.text: *None of* takes either a singular or a plural verb, and both are standard. Be consistent.
items.example: None of the proposals were affordable.

items.text: *All of* and *both of* follow the noun after them, so the verb is plural with a plural noun.
items.example: All of the equipment was returned undamaged.

body.heard: *Every* means all of them, so it takes a plural verb.
also_known_as: every is the same as all
body.truth: *Every* covers the whole group in meaning and stays singular in shape. English looks at the members one at a time here, so it is *every student receives*, never *every students receive*.
body.what_to_do: Use *all* with a plural noun and a plural verb. Use *every* with a singular noun and a singular verb. They mean the same and they behave differently.

body.text: Five forms of the same word, one per slot

English changes the shape of a pronoun depending on where it sits. Before the verb it takes one shape, after the verb another, and in front of a noun a third. The table has all five shapes for every person.
Read it across a row, not down a column. Each row is one person, and the five cells are the five places that person can appear in a sentence.

*His* fills two slots and does not change between them.
*Her* fills two slots: after a verb, and in front of a noun.
Written English uses the same *you* for one person and for several.

body.text: A pronoun is a promise that the reader can fill it in

A pronoun saves you from repeating a noun. It only works when the reader can put the noun back. If two nouns in the last sentence could fit, the reader has to guess, and half the time they guess wrong.

body.anchor_line: Every pronoun needs one, and it needs to be the only one that fits. When two nouns fit, the sentence has stopped saying anything definite.

body.text: How to stop a pronoun pointing at two things at once
The fix is not a rule about pronouns. It is a habit: when the noun you mean is not the only one that fits, put a noun after the pointing word. *This shift*, *these findings*, *that decision*.

body.lead_in: The same sentence three times. Each version tells the reader more about what *this* means.

body.text: What goes wrong when a pronoun is left loose

body.wrong: The council wrote to the contractor after it missed the deadline.
body.right: The council wrote to the contractor after the contractor missed the deadline.
body.why_it_happens: You know which one missed the deadline, so the pronoun feels clear. Two nouns in the sentence can both take *it*, and the reader has no way to choose between them.
body.smallest_fix: Repeat the noun, or rewrite so only one noun comes before the pronoun.

body.wrong: Rents rose and wages stayed flat. This is the main cause of the problem.
body.right: Rents rose and wages stayed flat. This gap is the main cause of the problem.
body.why_it_happens: *This* feels like a link back to the whole of the last sentence, and often it is. When the last sentence contains two ideas, the reader cannot tell which one you have picked up.
body.smallest_fix: Put a noun after *this*: *this gap*, *this rise*, *this pattern*.

body.wrong: Everyone in the department have been asked to comment.
body.right: Everyone in the department has been asked to comment.
body.why_it_happens: *Everyone* covers a whole group, and *department* is plural in your ear, so the plural verb comes out. *Everyone* is singular in shape, and the words in between do not change the verb.
body.smallest_fix: Cover the words between the pronoun and the verb. *Everyone has* is what is left.

body.heard: Never repeat a noun. Use a pronoun instead, or the writing looks repetitive.
also_known_as: repeating a word is bad style
body.truth: Repeating a key noun is what holds a paragraph together. Reaching for a pronoun every time is what produces sentences where nobody can tell what *it* means, and that costs far more than repetition does.
body.what_to_do: Use a pronoun when only one noun can fit it. When two could, repeat the noun, or put it after *this* or *these*.

articles.title: Where a describing word goes, and what order two of them take

article_json.also_called: Attributive and predicative adjectives, and adjective order
article_json.one_line: This tells you the two places a describing word can sit, the words that only fit one of them, and the order when you use several.
article_json.short_answer: Put the describing word in front of the noun, or after *be*, *seem* or *look*. With two of them, opinion comes before fact: *a useful new route*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: Where does a describing word go, and which one comes first when I have two?

body.text: Two places a describing word can sit

An adjective goes in one of two places. It sits directly in front of the noun, or it sits after *be*, *seem*, *look* and the other linking verbs. Most adjectives take either slot and mean the same thing in both.

body.caption: Same word, same meaning, two slots.
footnotes: The linking verbs are *be, seem, become, appear, feel, look, sound, taste, smell, remain, stay, get, turn, grow*. They all take an adjective, never an adverb.

body.lead_in: Only the slot changes. The describing word is the same in both.

items.text: A narrow footbridge crosses the canal at Verdon.
items.gloss: There is a footbridge there and it is not wide.

items.text: The footbridge at Verdon is narrow.
items.gloss: The same fact, with the describing word after the verb.

items.text: The estimate seems low for a job of this size.
items.gloss: You think the price they quoted is too small.

items.text: That roof looks unsafe to me, to be honest.
items.gloss: You would not want to walk on it.

body.so_what: Both slots carry the same meaning. Which one you use is a sentence-shape choice, not a meaning choice.

body.text: The words that only fit one of the two slots
Two short lists break the pattern. One group only goes in front of a noun. The other only goes after a linking verb. Both lists are closed, and both are worth learning as lists.

body.caption: Two closed lists, one for each slot.
headers: Only in front of a noun
footnotes: So *the main reason* works and *the reason is main* does not. *The child is asleep* works and *the asleep child* does not.
For the second list, use a different word in front of a noun: *a sleeping child*, *a frightened driver*, *a living language*.

body.text: Put the adjective in front of the noun, or after a linking verb. Two short lists take only one of the two slots.

body.lead_in: Each of these uses a word from one of the two closed lists in its only slot.

items.text: The main reason for the delay was a shortage of parts.
items.gloss: Missing parts held the work up more than anything else.

items.text: The former director now advises two other trusts.
items.gloss: The person who used to run it works elsewhere.

items.text: Half the passengers were asleep by the second stop.
items.gloss: Most people on the bus had dropped off early.

items.text: She's aware of the risk and she's going anyway.
items.gloss: She knows it is dangerous and has decided to go.

body.so_what: Each of those words has one slot and only one. Put it in the other slot and the sentence stops being English.

body.text: The order when you use more than one

When two or three describing words stack in front of a noun, English has a preferred order. What you think about the thing comes first. What the thing measurably is comes after, and the closer to the noun a word sits, the more permanent it is.

body.caption: Opinion first, then the facts, with the most permanent nearest the noun.
footnotes: *A striking large modern glass office block* uses slots 1, 2, 3, 7 and 8 in order.
Two or three describing words is plenty. Five is a style problem, not an achievement.

body.lead_in: One describing word is added each time, and the earlier ones do not move.

items.text: They have built a storage unit behind the depot.
items.gloss: There is a new place to keep things there.

items.text: They have built a steel storage unit behind the depot.
items.gloss: The same unit, and now you know what it is made of.

items.text: They have built a large steel storage unit behind the depot.
items.gloss: The same unit again, and it is a big one.

items.text: It's an ugly large steel storage unit, if you ask me.
items.gloss: You do not like the look of it.

body.so_what: Each new word went in at the front. What you think of the thing always ends up furthest from the noun.

body.term_or_structure: comparing two things with an adjective
body.one_line: To compare, English adds *-er* to a short adjective or *more* to a long one: *narrower*, *more expensive*. The full story is in [th_comparatives_and_superlatives].

body.text: What goes wrong with describing words

body.wrong: The council approved a scheme new for the town centre.
body.right: The council approved a new scheme for the town centre.
body.why_it_happens: Many languages put the describing word after the noun, and the sentence still makes sense that way, so nothing warns you. English puts it in front, with almost no exceptions.
body.smallest_fix: Move the describing word so it sits directly in front of its noun.

body.wrong: The proposal seems reasonably, given the budget.
body.right: The proposal seems reasonable, given the budget.
body.why_it_happens: *Seem* is a verb, and words that describe verbs usually end in *-ly*. After a linking verb the word is describing the subject, not the verb, so it stays an adjective.
body.smallest_fix: After *be*, *seem*, *look*, *sound*, *feel* or *become*, take the *-ly* off.

body.wrong: They replaced the olds windows on the north side.
body.right: They replaced the old windows on the north side.
body.why_it_happens: In many languages the describing word matches the noun for number. English describing words never change shape, whatever noun follows them.
body.smallest_fix: Take the *-s* off the describing word. Only the noun carries it.

body.what_varies: The order of the middle slots when several describing words stack.

option_a.label: the order most references give
option_a.form: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose
option_a.example: a striking large modern glass office block

option_b.label: the order some references give
option_b.form: opinion, size, physical quality, shape, age, colour, origin, material, type
option_b.example: a striking large smooth modern glass office block

body.why_this_default: The two agree on the ends and differ in the middle, and speakers move words for emphasis. This is a house choice for our examples. It is a strong tendency, not a law.

body.heard: There is a fixed order for adjectives and breaking it is a grammar mistake.
body.truth: It is a strong tendency, and references disagree about the middle of the list. A speaker who wants to stress one word will move it, and nobody hears an error. What sounds wrong is a phrase where opinion comes after fact: *a large ugly unit* is fine, *a steel ugly unit* is not.
body.what_to_do: Keep what you think of the thing furthest from the noun and what it is made of nearest. Then stop at three describing words.

body.headline: In front of the noun, or after a linking verb. Opinion first.
