article_json.one_line: This settles which ending to use, so you say who is feeling something and what is causing the feeling.
article_json.short_answer: *-ing* is what the thing does to you: *the delay was frustrating*. *-ed* is what you feel: *I was frustrated*. Only people and animals take *-ed*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: Do I say *I am bored* or *I am boring*?

body.text: Both endings are correct, and they say opposite things
*The lecture was boring* and *the students were bored* are both correct English, and they are not two ways of saying one thing. One names the cause, the other names the person who felt it.
So the choice is never about which word is better. It is about which end of the arrow you are describing: the thing that gives out the feeling, or the person who receives it.

body.question: Am I describing what causes the feeling, or who has it?

options.label: *-ing*
options.use_it_when: You are describing the thing, the event or the situation that produces the feeling.
options.example: The wait at the border was exhausting.

options.label: *-ed*
options.use_it_when: You are describing the person or animal who has the feeling.
options.example: The drivers were exhausted by the time they arrived.

b.means: The people running the study did not expect what they found.

a.text: I found the second lecture confusing.
a.means: The lecture itself was hard to follow.

b.text: I was confused by the second lecture.
b.means: You came out not understanding it.

a.means: Something about the journey wore people out.

b.means: The people on board had no energy left.

a.text: She is interesting to listen to.
a.means: Other people enjoy hearing her talk.

b.text: She is interested in coastal erosion.
b.means: That subject is what she wants to work on.

body.deciding_factor: Ask whether the thing you are describing can feel anything. If it cannot, the ending is *-ing*.
body.trap: You translate the sentence as one word in your own language, where a single form covers both jobs, so there is nothing in the sentence to warn you that English has split it in two.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere. The pair is most expensive in Speaking Part 1, where *I am boring* is a memorable thing to have said about yourself.

body.text: How the two endings are built

body.caption: One verb, two describing words, and the endings never swap jobs.
footnotes: The list is longer than these ten, and every member behaves the same way, so learning the pattern is enough.

body.caption: The feeling travels from the cause to the person.

body.text: Use *-ing* for the thing that causes the feeling. Use *-ed* for the person or animal that has it.

body.lead_in: Only what is being described changes. The ending follows it every time.

items.text: The figures in the third column are worrying.
items.gloss: Those numbers give people reason to worry.

items.text: The residents are worried about the third column.
items.gloss: The people living there feel anxious.

items.text: The final report was disappointing.
items.gloss: It was not as good as people had hoped.

items.text: Honestly, I was disappointed with the whole thing.
items.gloss: You had expected better and you did not get it.

body.so_what: Ask what the describing word is attached to. A thing takes *-ing*, a person takes *-ed*.

body.text: What goes wrong, and it is one error in two shapes

body.wrong: I was very boring during the first week of the course.
body.right: I was very bored during the first week of the course.
body.why_it_happens: You mean that you felt nothing was happening, and in many languages one word covers both halves. In English *-ing* makes you the cause, so the sentence says you were the dull thing.
body.smallest_fix: If the word describes a person's feeling, change *-ing* to *-ed*.

body.wrong: The waiting time at the health centre is frustrated.
body.right: The waiting time at the health centre is frustrating.
body.why_it_happens: The waiting time is where the frustration comes from, so it feels as though it should carry the same word as the feeling. Only something that can feel takes *-ed*.
body.smallest_fix: If the word describes a thing or a situation, change *-ed* to *-ing*.

body.heard: *-ing* words describe things and *-ed* words describe people.
also_known_as: ing for objects, ed for humans
body.truth: That gets the right answer most of the time and it hides the reason, so it breaks on sentences like *she is very interesting*. A person can perfectly well be the cause of a feeling, and then a person takes *-ing*.
body.what_to_do: Ask which end of the arrow you are describing. The one that gives out the feeling takes *-ing*, whether it is a person or a thing.

body.headline: *-ing* gives the feeling out. *-ed* receives it.
